questions.stem: During an immediate unit emergency, the charge nurse assigns specific roles and gives concise directions without first seeking a group vote. Which leadership style is being used?

options.text: Democratic
Servant
Autocratic
Laissez-faire

questions.correct_rationale: Autocratic behavior can be useful when rapid coordination is needed. Identifying the style does not imply it is the best approach for every setting; the urgency in this scenario explains its use.

option_rationales.A: This involves shared participation in decisions rather than the described directive response.
option_rationales.B: Serving and developing others may be a broader orientation, but it does not identify the directive decision pattern here.
option_rationales.C: The leader makes and directs the immediate decisions.
option_rationales.D: This gives the group substantial control with minimal direction.

questions.exam_strategy: Identify who makes the decision and how much immediate input the group provides.

questions.stem: A unit has several weeks to redesign its shift-report process. The manager brings staff together to compare proposals and shares planning decisions with them. Which style is most clearly shown?

options.text: Laissez-faire
Transactional
Autocratic
Democratic

questions.correct_rationale: Democratic leadership combines leader involvement with meaningful group participation. It differs from laissez-faire because the manager still structures and shares the decision process rather than largely stepping back.

option_rationales.A: The manager remains actively involved in a structured collaborative process.
option_rationales.B: The stem does not base participation on a reward-for-performance exchange.
option_rationales.C: The manager is not making the plan alone and issuing it to the group.
option_rationales.D: The defining feature is staff participation in planning and decision-making.

questions.exam_strategy: Participation with active leader involvement points to democratic leadership.

questions.stem: Which team is most likely to work effectively with substantial independence and minimal day-to-day direction?

options.text: A newly assembled team unfamiliar with essential safety procedures.
A team managing a rapidly unfolding emergency with unclear roles.
Experienced, motivated staff doing familiar work with clear goals.
A team with persistent unresolved conflict and missed deadlines.

questions.correct_rationale: Laissez-faire leadership can work when team members have the knowledge and motivation to guide their work. Independence still requires goals, boundaries, and access to resources; it is not abandonment of leadership responsibility.

option_rationales.A: This team needs orientation and closer direction before independent work.
option_rationales.B: Urgency and role uncertainty require active coordination.
option_rationales.C: Competence, motivation, and established expectations support independent work.
option_rationales.D: Minimal direction is unlikely to resolve these existing performance barriers.

questions.exam_strategy: Match the level of direction to team readiness and the predictability of the task.

questions.stem: A nurse leader builds a shared vision for safer care, invites staff to design improvements, and mentors nurses who lead the changes. Which theory best describes this approach?

options.text: Transformational
Transactional
Scientific management
Laissez-faire

questions.correct_rationale: Transformational leadership seeks commitment through meaning, vision, and growth. Staff participation alone is not the full clue; the combined emphasis on inspiration and development distinguishes the theory here.

option_rationales.A: Shared purpose, empowerment, and development are the defining features.
option_rationales.B: The scenario does not rely primarily on contingent rewards or discipline.
option_rationales.C: The emphasis is not finding the fastest task method or pay by output.
option_rationales.D: The leader is actively inspiring and mentoring rather than providing minimal direction.

questions.exam_strategy: Look for vision and empowerment when distinguishing transformational leadership.

questions.stem: A manager tells staff that completing a defined training target will earn a specified reward and that missed requirements will trigger the established corrective process. Which approach is most evident?

options.text: Transactional
Ethics of care
Laissez-faire
Transformational

questions.correct_rationale: Transactional leadership organizes work through structure and exchanges tied to performance. Rewards are not automatically inappropriate; the question asks which mechanism is used to guide behavior.

option_rationales.A: The relationship uses explicit performance expectations and contingent consequences.
option_rationales.B: This is an ethical framework, not the leadership exchange being described.
option_rationales.C: The manager is defining expectations and consequences rather than stepping back.
option_rationales.D: A shared inspiring vision and personal development are not the central mechanisms described.

questions.exam_strategy: An explicit performance-for-reward exchange points to transactional leadership.

questions.stem: A charge nurse closely coaches a novice on a new task, but gives an experienced nurse greater independence with familiar work. What best explains this difference?

options.text: Laissez-faire leadership for the entire team
Inconsistent standards of safe care
Reward power
Situational leadership

questions.correct_rationale: Situational leadership adapts the approach to the person, task, and environment. Fair leadership does not require identical direction for every team member when their preparation differs.

option_rationales.A: The novice is receiving active direction, so one minimal-direction style does not fit both.
option_rationales.B: Varying supervision can support the same safety standard when readiness differs.
option_rationales.C: The difference is based on readiness, not a promised benefit for compliance.
option_rationales.D: The amount of direction changes with competence and the demands of the task.

questions.exam_strategy: Different support can be appropriate when the underlying needs differ.

questions.stem: After receiving criticism, a charge nurse notices becoming defensive, pauses, and asks for specific examples before responding calmly. Which capability is most directly demonstrated?

options.text: Coercive power
Scientific management
Emotional intelligence
Avoidance of conflict

questions.correct_rationale: Self-awareness and self-management are central components of emotional intelligence. Pausing to regulate emotion while continuing the discussion supports constructive interaction; calm engagement differs from ignoring a conflict.

option_rationales.A: Coercive power relies on threatened consequences; the nurse instead regulates emotion and seeks clarification.
option_rationales.B: The response is not a task-efficiency or output calculation.
option_rationales.C: The nurse recognizes and regulates an emotional response while preserving communication.
option_rationales.D: The nurse remains engaged and requests information rather than withdrawing.

questions.exam_strategy: Look for recognition and management of emotion, not simply the absence of emotion.

questions.stem: Which action most directly illustrates the formal manager's resource-allocation responsibility?

options.text: Encourage a colleague to pursue a long-term career goal.
Demonstrate a skill to a new employee during orientation.
Inspire peers to support a shared professional goal without formal authority.
Adjust staffing assignments to match workload and available competencies.

questions.correct_rationale: Leadership and management often overlap, but the question identifies a specific management function. Matching staff resources to workload and competence is operational resource allocation, regardless of whether the manager also inspires the team.

option_rationales.A: Illustrates mentoring or development rather than the specific allocation function.
option_rationales.B: Illustrates precepting or teaching rather than staffing allocation.
option_rationales.C: Influencing peers toward a shared purpose illustrates informal leadership rather than formal allocation of resources.
option_rationales.D: Allocates personnel resources as part of formal operational management.

questions.exam_strategy: Classify the action being performed rather than relying on the person's title.

questions.stem: A new graduate has a designated nurse who supervises unit orientation and verifies current skills. A different nurse meets monthly to discuss long-term career development. Which pairing best fits these roles?

options.text: Orientation nurse: preceptor; career guide: mentor.
Orientation nurse: mentor only; career guide: preceptor.
Both are mentees because both participate in learning relationships.
Both are managers because both offer advice.

questions.correct_rationale: A preceptor typically supports entry into a specific role and immediate clinical competence. A mentor generally supports a broader developmental relationship; one person can sometimes do both, but the described functions are distinct.

option_rationales.A: Separates structured role preparation from broader professional development.
option_rationales.B: Reverses the characteristic focus of the two roles.
option_rationales.C: A mentee is the recipient of mentoring, not the guiding role described.
option_rationales.D: Advice does not itself confer a formal management position.

questions.exam_strategy: Ask whether the focus is learning this role now or developing a career over time.

questions.stem: Nurses seek a staff nurse's advice about complex equipment because of that nurse's extensive technical knowledge. The nurse has no formal authority over them. Which power source is most directly demonstrated?

options.text: Coercive power
Reward power
Expert power
Legitimate power

questions.correct_rationale: Expert power rests on perceived competence rather than title. The specific clue is why coworkers seek advice: technical knowledge, not authority, rewards, or threatened consequences.

option_rationales.A: No threat of punishment explains the team's response.
option_rationales.B: No ability to provide a benefit is the stated reason for influence.
option_rationales.C: Influence comes from recognized knowledge and skill.
option_rationales.D: This comes from an official position, which the stem excludes.

questions.exam_strategy: Identify the source of influence, not whether the person is influential.

questions.stem: A nurse preparing for leadership lists "I am skilled at resolving team disagreements" and "A nearby university now offers a leadership certificate." How should these be classified in a SWOT analysis?

options.text: Both are threats because both involve change.
Conflict-resolution skill: strength; available certificate program: opportunity.
Conflict-resolution skill: opportunity; certificate program: strength.
Both are strengths because both could help the nurse.

questions.correct_rationale: SWOT separates internal strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats. A nurse's current skill is internal; a newly available educational pathway exists outside the nurse and can be used for development.

option_rationales.A: Neither statement identifies a negative external condition.
option_rationales.B: The skill is an internal asset; the new program is an external possibility.
option_rationales.C: This reverses the distinction: an existing personal skill is internal, while an available program is external.
option_rationales.D: Usefulness alone does not distinguish internal from external factors.

questions.exam_strategy: First sort internal versus external, then helpful versus harmful.

questions.stem: Two nurses disagree about how to share routine duties. There is no immediate safety threat. Each has accused the other of not helping. What is the manager's best initial approach?

options.text: Privately clarify concerns and identify a shared goal.
Ignore the conflict until one nurse requests a transfer.
Assign each nurse exactly half the duties before discussing why the current arrangement is failing.
Announce in front of the unit that both nurses are unprofessional.

questions.correct_rationale: Conflict resolution begins with understanding the problem and the parties' interests. A private, specific discussion supports a workable shared solution; premature judgment or public blame makes collaboration less likely.

option_rationales.A: Creates a respectful setting for understanding interests before negotiating a solution.
option_rationales.B: Allows a potentially manageable problem to persist without constructive engagement.
option_rationales.C: Equal task counts may not address unequal demands or the causes of conflict; clarification should come first.
option_rationales.D: Public blame can intensify defensiveness and does not clarify the problem.

questions.exam_strategy: For nonurgent interpersonal conflict, clarify facts and goals before imposing a solution.

questions.stem: A manager is preparing staff for a new handoff process before implementation. Which actions support readiness for change? Select all that apply.

options.text: Share the problem the change is intended to address.
Connect the proposed change to a shared patient-care goal.
Invite staff concerns and identify barriers to participation.
Assume silence means agreement and skip discussion.

questions.correct_rationale: Preparing for change involves explaining the need and addressing concerns before expecting adoption. This supports unfreezing and readiness; it differs from merely announcing a completed decision and interpreting quietness as acceptance.

option_rationales.A: Builds understanding of why current practice needs reconsideration.
option_rationales.B: Gives the change a meaningful purpose for the team.
option_rationales.C: Understanding concerns reveals practical barriers and helps the manager address resistance before implementation.
option_rationales.D: Silence does not establish understanding or commitment.

questions.exam_strategy: Match actions to the phase: preparing for change comes before routine integration.

questions.stem: At the start of a shift, a nurse has routine documentation, a stable patient awaiting a bath, and a patient reporting new shortness of breath. Which actions support safe time management? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess the new breathing complaint promptly and activate needed help.
Delegate appropriate routine care to a competent team member with clear instructions.
Reassess priorities as new information becomes available.
Complete tasks in the order written regardless of changes in condition.

questions.correct_rationale: Time management in nursing is guided by patient needs, not merely by completing a list quickly. Addressing an acute change, using appropriate delegation, and reprioritizing allow routine work to proceed without ignoring risk.

option_rationales.A: A potentially urgent change takes priority over routine work.
option_rationales.B: Uses available resources while retaining nursing judgment and follow-up.
option_rationales.C: Safe organization is dynamic rather than limited to a once-per-shift plan.
option_rationales.D: A fixed list does not accommodate changing urgency.

questions.exam_strategy: Urgency and changing condition override routine sequence.

questions.stem: A manager wants to develop staff and remove barriers to their work. Which actions fit servant leadership and empowerment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take credit for staff ideas while withholding information needed to use them.
Require staff to seek permission for every routine decision they are qualified to make.
Provide coaching and appropriate decision-making authority with support.
Obtain needed resources so staff can implement a safe improvement they designed.

questions.correct_rationale: Servant leadership values and develops others; empowerment gives people meaningful ability to act. Resources, coaching, and appropriate authority support that ability, while excessive control and withholding information undermine it.

option_rationales.A: Taking credit and withholding information undermine the trust and participation needed for empowerment.
option_rationales.B: Unnecessarily limits autonomy rather than empowering competent staff.
option_rationales.C: Develops confidence and autonomy within clear responsibilities.
option_rationales.D: Supports staff initiative by removing an operational barrier.

questions.exam_strategy: Look for practical support that enables others to contribute and grow.

questions.stem: The RN has assessed four patients. Facility policy permits trained UAP to provide routine hygiene and collect intake and output. Which task is most appropriate to delegate to a competent UAP?

options.text: Develop the initial fluid-management teaching plan.
Decide whether a new diuretic dose was effective.
Measure and record the urine output of a stable patient according to the established plan.
Determine why a patient's urine output has fallen sharply.

questions.correct_rationale: Delegation depends on the task, patient condition, competence, and permitted role. Collecting a measurement in an established plan can be delegated here; deciding what the measurement means remains a nursing responsibility.

option_rationales.B: Requires nursing evaluation of the patient's response.
option_rationales.C: Involves routine data collection within the stated policy and competence.
option_rationales.D: Requires assessment and clinical interpretation rather than collection alone.

questions.stem: After assessing a stable patient, the RN delegates routine vital signs to a competent UAP. Which instruction is most complete?

options.text: "At 1000, record the values; report values outside these limits or new symptoms immediately."
"Take the vital signs and decide whether the scheduled medicine should be held."

"Take the usual observations whenever convenient and tell me if you think I should review them."

questions.correct_rationale: Clear directions tell the delegatee what to do, when to do it, and what to report. Patient-specific parameters reduce ambiguity while the RN retains responsibility for interpretation and follow-up.

option_rationales.A: Specifies task, timing, documentation, and circumstances requiring prompt reporting.
option_rationales.B: Adds a clinical treatment decision beyond routine measurement.
option_rationales.C: Specifies timing but delays concerns that may require prompt attention.
option_rationales.D: Leaves timing and report criteria to the delegatee without clear patient-specific direction.

questions.exam_strategy: A complete direction includes the task, time, limits, and reporting expectations.

questions.stem: The RN delegates an established repositioning schedule to a competent UAP for a stable patient at risk for skin injury. At the end of the interval, what remains an RN responsibility?

options.text: Assume the plan worked if every scheduled turn was recorded.
Evaluate the skin response and adjust the nursing plan.
End monitoring because the task was appropriately delegated.
Ask the UAP to independently stage a new skin injury and select treatment.

questions.correct_rationale: The delegatee can report observations and task completion, but the RN evaluates the clinical outcome. Delegation changes who performs a task; it does not eliminate ongoing nursing judgment about whether the plan is effective.

option_rationales.A: Task completion does not establish the patient outcome.
option_rationales.B: Determining effectiveness and adjusting the plan require nursing judgment.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate delegation still requires supervision and evaluation.
option_rationales.D: Transfers clinical assessment and treatment planning beyond the routine task.

questions.exam_strategy: Distinguish a task being completed from the desired outcome being achieved.

questions.stem: An RN appropriately delegates a routine task to a competent UAP and provides directions. Which statement best describes accountability?

options.text: The UAP has no accountability because a nurse delegated the task.
The RN transfers every responsibility for the patient to the UAP.
The RN remains accountable for the delegation decision and appropriate oversight; the UAP is accountable for performing and reporting within the accepted role.
The RN must personally perform every delegated step for accountability to exist.

questions.correct_rationale: Delegation creates related responsibilities rather than making either team member solely responsible for everything. The RN must make and oversee a sound delegation decision, while the UAP must perform the accepted task competently and communicate concerns.

option_rationales.A: The delegatee remains responsible for accepted performance and reporting.
option_rationales.B: Delegation does not transfer the RN's overall nursing judgment and oversight.
option_rationales.C: Recognizes distinct responsibilities for both members of the team.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate delegation permits another competent person to perform the task with suitable oversight.

questions.exam_strategy: Avoid answers that assign all responsibility to one person or none to the other.

questions.stem: A UAP reports a newly low blood pressure and that the patient feels faint. The RN is completing routine paperwork. What is the best response?

options.text: Assess the patient promptly and arrange help as indicated.
Finish the paperwork before checking because the UAP has already taken the vital signs.
Ask the UAP to determine whether the medication caused the problem.
Have the UAP repeat the measurement in 30 minutes before interrupting routine work.

questions.correct_rationale: The UAP has fulfilled an important reporting role by communicating the value and symptoms. The RN must now interpret and assess the change; routine data collection is not a substitute for clinical evaluation.

option_rationales.A: New symptoms with an abnormal measurement require timely RN interpretation and action.
option_rationales.B: Routine work does not take priority over a potentially significant change.
option_rationales.C: Determining the cause requires clinical interpretation and assessment beyond the UAP's role in collecting and reporting data.
option_rationales.D: A delayed repeat does not address faintness and the newly low pressure; prompt assessment is needed.

questions.exam_strategy: When abnormal data come with new symptoms, prioritize the patient over routine tasks.

questions.stem: A UAP is competent in routine feeding assistance. Which patient is the best candidate for that task under a policy permitting feeding assistance for stable patients with an established safe feeding plan?

options.text: A patient who has become unusually drowsy since the last meal.
A patient who has just developed coughing with every sip.
A newly admitted patient whose swallowing safety has not yet been assessed.
A stable patient with an established feeding plan, needing hand assistance.

questions.correct_rationale: The task name alone does not establish safety. Feeding can be routine for a stable patient with an assessed plan, while new coughing, drowsiness, or an unassessed swallowing status changes the circumstances.

option_rationales.A: A changed level of alertness requires evaluation before feeding assistance.
option_rationales.B: New swallowing symptoms require assessment before routine feeding continues.
option_rationales.C: The established safe plan required in the stem is missing.
option_rationales.D: Needs routine physical assistance within the stated plan.

questions.exam_strategy: Apply patient-specific risk before deciding that a familiar task is routine.

options.text: A stable patient needing established dressings and routine oral medicines.
A patient needing independent RN-level triage of several new symptoms.
A new patient whose initial comprehensive nursing assessment and plan are incomplete.
A patient with a rapidly changing condition requiring repeated comprehensive assessment.

questions.correct_rationale: The best assignment matches patient predictability, permitted scope, and demonstrated competence. The stem supplies those permissions explicitly because specific LPN/LVN activities vary across jurisdictions and settings.

option_rationales.B: The task specifically requires RN judgment rather than the permitted routine care.
option_rationales.C: Initial comprehensive assessment and planning remain with the RN in this scenario.

questions.stem: A unit policy lists a task as delegable, but the RN identifies that the applicable nursing regulations prohibit delegating it to that worker category. What should the RN do?

options.text: Follow the policy because facility rules always override nursing regulations.
Use an authorized person and clarify the conflicting policy.
Delegate if the worker has done the task successfully before.
Delegate if the patient agrees to the worker performing it.

questions.correct_rationale: Safe delegation must satisfy both applicable law and organizational requirements. A permissive policy or past successful performance cannot authorize an activity that the governing regulation excludes.

option_rationales.A: Reverses the legal relationship between policy and regulation.
option_rationales.B: Facility policy cannot expand a worker's authority beyond applicable law.
option_rationales.C: Experience does not override a legal prohibition.
option_rationales.D: Patient agreement does not create professional authority that law prohibits.

questions.exam_strategy: Competence and consent do not replace legal authority.

questions.concept: Workload and ability to accept a task
questions.stem: A competent UAP says a newly delegated task cannot be completed by the requested time because of several other patient-care duties. What is the RN's best response?

options.text: Remove the task from the care plan because there is insufficient time.
Document that the UAP is uncooperative without discussing the conflict.
Review priorities and redistribute work to meet care needs.
Repeat the instruction more firmly and consider the task accepted.

questions.correct_rationale: Right-person decisions include practical ability to carry out the task within the needed time, not only technical skill. Communication about workload allows the RN to reprioritize and secure care rather than leave an impossible assignment unresolved.

option_rationales.A: Staffing constraints alone do not establish that the patient no longer needs the care.
option_rationales.B: Labels the worker without evaluating the reported constraint.
option_rationales.C: Checks actual capacity and creates a feasible plan rather than assuming refusal.
option_rationales.D: Does not resolve the stated workload barrier or confirm completion is feasible.

questions.exam_strategy: When a delegatee reports a barrier, resolve feasibility and priorities before assuming completion.

questions.stem: An RN is considering delegating routine ambulation. Which checks support a sound delegation decision? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume a task is delegable whenever it saves the RN time.
Provide clear directions and a plan for reporting and follow-up.
Confirm that the patient's current condition makes the task appropriate.
Verify the delegatee's competence and permitted role.

questions.correct_rationale: The five rights consider task, circumstance, person, directions/communication, and supervision/evaluation. A delegation decision must meet the relevant safety conditions; convenience is not sufficient. The proposed ambulation must be suitable for this patient now, assigned to a competent person, and accompanied by clear reporting and follow-up expectations.

option_rationales.A: Efficiency alone does not establish any of the required safety conditions.
option_rationales.B: Clear directions and reporting expectations support communication, while planned follow-up supports supervision and evaluation.
option_rationales.C: Checking current stability and suitability addresses the right circumstance rather than relying on an earlier assessment.
option_rationales.D: Addresses the right person and whether the task is authorized.

questions.exam_strategy: Run the whole delegation checklist rather than stopping at a familiar task name.

questions.stem: In this setting, UAP may collect routine data and provide established basic care. Which activities should the RN retain rather than delegate to UAP? Select all that apply.

options.text: Evaluate whether a patient has achieved a teaching outcome.
Measure routine intake using an established method for a stable patient.
Complete the initial comprehensive nursing assessment.
Determine whether new symptoms require a change in the nursing plan.

questions.correct_rationale: The boundary is the need for nursing judgment, not whether an activity involves interacting with a patient. Routine measurements may be delegated here, but assessment, planning decisions, and outcome evaluation remain with the RN.

option_rationales.A: Requires professional evaluation rather than reporting that teaching occurred.
option_rationales.B: This is permitted routine data collection in the setting described.
option_rationales.C: Requires professional nursing assessment rather than basic data collection.
option_rationales.D: Interpreting new symptoms and changing the care plan require nursing judgment beyond routine data collection.

questions.exam_strategy: Look for verbs such as interpret, determine, plan, and evaluate.

questions.stem: The RN has assessed the patients, established care plans, and verified UAP competence. Policy allows routine hygiene, weights, and urine specimen collection for stable patients. Which tasks may be delegated? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assist a stable patient with bathing while following the documented assistance level.
Obtain a scheduled weight for a stable patient using the prescribed method.
Collect a routine clean-catch urine specimen after the patient has received needed instruction.
Determine why a patient has new difficulty urinating and select an intervention.

questions.correct_rationale: The scenario supplies the assessments, policies, and competence needed for these routine tasks. The remaining option adds interpretation of a new symptom and selection of an intervention, which changes the required professional role.

option_rationales.A: Is basic care matched to an assessed need.
option_rationales.B: Is routine measurement within the established plan.
option_rationales.C: Is permitted specimen collection under the stated conditions.
option_rationales.D: Requires clinical assessment and choice of treatment, not specimen collection.

questions.exam_strategy: Read the full action; a routine task can become nondelegable when judgment is added.
